strengths: The paper addresses a useful and challenging vision problem: identifying added, removed, and moved object instances across captures with different viewpoints. Under the default Algorithms/General assessment, both the integrated method and the substantial benchmark contribution support a slight preference for acceptance.

SceneDiff provides 350 real-world video pairs across 50 scenes and 20 scene categories, with 1,009 annotated objects. Combining deliberately collected scenes with naturally occurring kitchen changes adds useful diversity. The SAM2-assisted annotation and manual refinement workflow is clearly described.

The method is coherent and technically motivated. Joint reconstruction establishes a shared coordinate system; asymmetric depth comparison addresses occlusion; and reprojected appearance features, region matching, and instance association provide complementary information without task-specific training.

The quantitative improvements are substantial. Per-view AP increases from 26.9 to 49.6 on SD-V and from 10.8 to 23.6 on SD-K relative to CYWS-3D. External RC-3D evaluation using conventional bounding-box AP50 also supports effectiveness: 68.7 versus 50.0 for CYWS-3D with sensor depth. ChangeSim provides additional evidence beyond the proposed benchmark.

The backbone and feature-cue ablations help explain the results, particularly the importance of accurate geometry for appearance reprojection. The supplement provides useful runtime measurements, baseline adaptations, threshold sensitivity, and concrete failure analyses involving repeated objects, limited overlap, and lighting changes.
weaknesses: The proposed evaluation only partially validates the stated multiview instance output. Matching a prediction centroid to a ground-truth bounding box is permissive, allowing a point outside the actual object mask to count as correct. Per-scene evaluation uses only the highest-confidence observation, so incorrect associations or missing masks in other views can escape evaluation. Allowing a second detection without penalty also weakens the test of deduplication. Complementary mask/box overlap and cross-view association metrics, plus sensitivity to duplicate tolerance, would strengthen the benchmark.

The dataset split is insufficiently specified. Section 3 gives validation/test counts but does not establish separation by physical scene, source recording, or HD-EPIC participant/kitchen. This matters because multiple recordings of one scene can generate multiple pairs, as the collection instructions explicitly permit. The manuscript also lacks a quantitative annotation-quality audit or agreement measurement. These omissions limit confidence in benchmark independence and label reliability.

The multiview comparison lacks a competitive per-scene baseline: VLM and 3DGS-CD scores are near zero, while the strongest baseline, CYWS-3D, is evaluated only per view. Applying the proposed association stage to CYWS-3D detections would help isolate the contribution of change scoring from association. Several relevant recent approaches cited in related work are also not evaluated. The external RC-3D result mitigates, but does not resolve, this concern.

The ablations emphasize backbone and cue selection rather than the central multiview design choices. There are no quantitative removals of frame pairing, asymmetric visibility handling, voxel aggregation, or instance association. Table 4 also shows that adding region matching to geometry-plus-appearance changes per-scene AP only from 45.5 to 46.3 and APtype from 25.1 to 25.5. Thus, the evidence supports the overall pipeline more strongly than the necessity of all its components.

Some implementation details remain ambiguous despite the substantial supplement: backbone variants, image resolution, voxel size, object-level confidence aggregation, and conflict resolution when several objects satisfy the cross-video appearance threshold are not specified. Equation 4 also uses the raw geometry score although the surrounding discussion describes visibility filtering. These details affect reproducibility and moved-object matching, whose APtype remains considerably below type-agnostic AP.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful computer-vision problem: detecting and associating changed objects across captures with different viewpoints. Although no contribution type is declared, the default Algorithms/General assessment should recognize the substantial benchmark contribution alongside the method.

SceneDiff provides 350 real video pairs from 50 scenes, with 1,009 annotated objects, dense masks, and change-type labels. Combining deliberately collected scenes with naturally occurring kitchen changes is valuable. The annotation interface and planned release could support further research on multiview spatial understanding.

The training-free pipeline is technically motivated: joint reconstruction establishes a shared coordinate system, directional depth comparisons distinguish disappearance from occlusion, and region-level appearance features improve robustness. The manuscript clearly explains most components and attributes its pretrained models and association procedure.

The quantitative improvements are substantial. Per-view AP increases from 26.9 to 49.6 on SD-V and from 10.8 to 23.6 on SD-K. On the existing RC-3D benchmark, SceneDiff achieves 68.7 AP50 versus 50.0 for CYWS-3D with sensor depth. This external evaluation provides evidence beyond the authors' new benchmark.

The supplement adds useful backbone and cue ablations, threshold sensitivity, runtime measurements, and concrete failure analyses. The discussion of identical-object ambiguity and reconstruction failures is appropriately candid. Overall, the benchmark and demonstrated gains support a slight preference for acceptance.
weaknesses: The proposed evaluation measures a narrower capability than the stated output of object masks across all visible views. A centroid inside a ground-truth bounding box counts as correct, a second detection is ignored, and per-scene matching uses only the highest-confidence point. Consequently, poor masks, incomplete tracks, and some duplicate instances can escape penalty. These choices reasonably accommodate heterogeneous outputs, but complementary localization/association metrics and sensitivity to duplicate tolerance are needed to substantiate the broader claims.

Dataset independence and annotation reliability are insufficiently documented. The paper specifies a split by video-pair count but does not establish whether scenes, source recordings, or HD-Epic participants are disjoint. This matters because the collection instructions explicitly encourage forming multiple pairs from the same scene. The annotation review workflow is described, but quantitative quality auditing and policies for visually unverifiable or ambiguous changes are missing.

The multiview comparison provides limited evidence against competitive alternatives for scene-level association: VLM and 3DGS-CD scores are near zero, while CYWS-3D is evaluated only per view. The authors make reasonable adaptations to help these baselines, but adding their association stage to CYWS-3D, or comparing against a simpler matched-backbone object-matching pipeline, would better isolate the method's contribution. Relevant recent methods cited in the related work are also absent from the main comparisons.

Several design choices receive limited validation. Table 4 shows that geometry plus reprojected appearance nearly matches the full method, while removing geometry yields slightly better type-aware AP. There is no direct ablation of directional visibility masking, voxel aggregation, or the association procedure. Cross-video identity matching uses a similarity threshold without a specified one-to-one assignment, leaving repeated-object handling unclear.

Change classification remains weak: per-scene AP falls from 46.3 to 25.5 when types are required on SD-V, and from 20.9 to 12.2 on SD-K. Per-change-type results would help distinguish missed detections from identity-matching failures. The robot example is a useful demonstration, but lacks repeated-trial success measurements and does not establish deployment reliability.

Reproduction still requires implementation details such as exact backbone variants, image resolutions, SAM proposal settings, voxel size, and the multiview VLM model size. Runtime is approximately 159 seconds per pair on an A40, which also limits the immediate interactive applicability of the demonstrated system.

strengths: The paper addresses an important vision problem: detecting object changes across captures with different viewpoints while maintaining object identities across views. Under the default Algorithms/General category, the combination of a useful benchmark and an effective method supports acceptance despite the reservations below.

SceneDiff provides 350 real-world video pairs and 1009 annotated objects, including both varied environments and naturally occurring kitchen changes. Dense instance annotations, change-type labels, and per-scene evaluation offer meaningful capabilities beyond per-image change detection. The SAM2-assisted annotation interface is also a useful contribution.

The training-free pipeline is coherent and technically motivated. Joint reconstruction, directional occlusion handling, reprojected appearance comparisons, and region association address complementary challenges. The contribution lies principally in their effective integration rather than a new foundational model.

The reported improvements are substantial: per-view AP increases from 26.9 to 49.6 on SD-V and from 10.8 to 23.6 on SD-K relative to CYWS-3D. On the independent RC-3D benchmark, SceneDiff achieves 68.7 AP50 versus 50.0 for CYWS-3D with sensor depth. The additional ChangeSim result provides evidence beyond the proposed evaluation protocol.

The manuscript provides informative backbone and feature ablations, threshold sensitivity analysis, runtime measurements, and concrete failure cases. Its discussion of identical-object ambiguity, reconstruction failures, and lighting changes appropriately qualifies the claims. The robot demonstration illustrates potential utility without constituting the main experimental evidence.
weaknesses: The proposed evaluation only partially measures the stated multiview output. Matching a prediction's highest-confidence point to a ground-truth box does not verify segmentation accuracy or consistent localization across its other views. Allowing a second detection per object without penalty further weakens sensitivity to fragmented identities. The rationale is reasonable for coarse detection, but complementary mask/box overlap and cross-view association metrics, plus sensitivity to duplicate tolerance, are needed to substantiate the full object-level claims.

Dataset independence and annotation reliability are insufficiently documented. The paper specifies validation/test pair counts but does not establish whether scenes, source videos, or HD-Epic participants are disjoint. This matters because collection permits multiple recordings of the same scene to generate additional pairs. Annotation review is described, but no quantitative quality audit is reported. The promised release 'for any use' also needs clarification regarding the inherited HD-Epic terms.

Comparative coverage is limited. The multiview baselines are dominated by a rendering method poorly suited to these captures and a VLM-plus-grounding pipeline with near-zero AP; CYWS-3D is not evaluated per scene. Comparisons with relevant recent zero-shot/correspondence approaches cited in the paper, or CYWS-3D combined with a shared association backend, would better establish the strength of the multiview contribution. The efforts to improve baseline inputs are nevertheless appreciated.

Table 4 does not isolate view pairing, directional visibility masking, voxel aggregation, or instance association. Moreover, removing the region cue nearly preserves per-scene AP (45.5 versus 46.3), while removing the geometry cue improves APtype (26.4 versus 25.5). Thus, the evidence supports the overall pipeline more strongly than the necessity of every component. Ablations are confined to SD-V, leaving their behavior on the harder kitchen subset uncertain.

Some implementation details remain underspecified, including exact foundation-model variants, voxel resolution, mask partitioning, and resolution of competing cross-sequence object matches. The appearance-only matching rule is particularly vulnerable to repeated objects, consistent with the considerably lower type-aware AP. These omissions limit reproducibility until the promised code release.

strengths: The benchmark addresses a meaningful gap: instance-consistent change detection across videos with different camera trajectories. Its 350 sequence pairs from 50 scenes, including naturally occurring kitchen changes, provide useful diversity. Splitting by physical scene reduces leakage, and the scene-level metric encourages consistent object identification rather than isolated per-frame detections.

The training-free method is technically well motivated. Joint reconstruction provides a common coordinate system, directional depth comparison distinguishes visible changes from occlusions, and region-level appearance features support object-centric reasoning. The constituent models and association approach are appropriately attributed.

The experimental gains are substantial. On SD-V/SD-K, SceneDiff achieves 43.8/20.9 object-per-image AP versus 24.5/16.8 for fine-tuned CYWS-2D. RC-3D results improve from 50.0 to 65.3 AP50 even against the sensor-depth baseline. Additional evaluations on PASLCD and ChangeSim support transfer beyond the proposed benchmark without dataset-specific parameter changes.

The supplementary material provides valuable baseline adaptation details, runtime measurements, threshold sensitivity analyses, and failure examples. Evaluating on PASLCD helps address concerns that sparse, different-trajectory inputs disadvantage rendering-based baselines. The discussion of indistinguishable objects and reconstruction failures is candid and informative.
weaknesses: The ablations do not fully establish the contribution of the proposed pipeline beyond its strong pretrained components. Table 5 does not isolate region pooling, voxel-based consistency, or video-level association. Moreover, removing the geometric change score improves scene-level AP by 2.6 points, and the reprojected appearance cue alone matches the full method's scene-level AP. These results weaken the case for the complete scoring formulation. The claim that newer foundation models naturally improve results also needs qualification: DINOv1/v2 outperform DINOv3 on object-per-image AP.

The strongest scene-level claim lacks a competitive controlled baseline. Table 2 compares scene-level AP only against the VLM pipeline and 3DGS-CD, which perform poorly even at per-image detection. Applying the same association procedure to a stronger per-frame baseline would help distinguish improvements in detecting changes from improvements in maintaining object identity.

The benchmark's annotation policy needs more precision around its central notion of 'verifiable' change. The manuscript does not clearly specify how changes known to collectors but unobservable because of occlusion, missing coverage, or identical-object substitutions are excluded or scored. Manual review is described, but there is no quantified annotation audit or agreement measurement. These details matter for interpreting scene-level errors and reproducibly extending the benchmark.

The primary scene-level metric is change-type agnostic, although predicting Added, Removed, and Moved is central to the task. The supplement appropriately reports type-aware AP, but it falls from 22.8/10.6 to 18.5/7.7 on SD-V/SD-K. Those results deserve main-paper prominence. The exact aggregation formula for cross-frame IoU should also be explicit, since pixel-summed and frame-averaged formulations weight object visibility differently.

The practical evidence supports feasibility more strongly than deployment readiness. Scene-level accuracy remains limited, average processing takes 159.4 seconds per sequence pair, and the robot demonstration lacks repeated-trial success statistics or a demonstrated feedback-based correction protocol to substantiate the 'closed-loop' description. These limitations do not negate the benchmark and detection contributions, but narrow the application claims.

strengths: Assessed as Algorithms/General, the paper offers a valuable combination of a benchmark and a practical method. SceneDiff addresses a meaningful gap: instance-consistent change detection across videos with different camera trajectories. Its 350 sequence pairs from 50 scenes, including naturally occurring changes from HD-Epic, substantially expand the evaluation setting beyond the small existing multiview datasets.

The method is technically well motivated. Joint geometric registration, directional visibility reasoning, region-level appearance comparison, and cross-view association form a coherent training-free pipeline. The paper appropriately attributes its pretrained components and association procedure.

The empirical evidence supports useful performance gains. On SD-V, SceneDiff achieves 43.8 object/image AP versus 24.5 for finetuned CYWS-2D; on SD-K, the corresponding scores are 20.9 versus 16.8. Evaluation on RC-3D, PASLCD, and ChangeSim provides evidence beyond the authors' benchmark, although gains on the latter two are smaller.

The supplement materially strengthens the submission through implementation details, runtime measurements, hyperparameter studies, change-type-aware evaluation, and explicit failure analyses. Scene-disjoint validation/test splits and manual review of propagated annotations are sensible choices. The discussion of repetitive objects, geometric failures, and unobservable identity changes is candid and useful.
weaknesses: The ablations do not establish the benefit of the complete scoring formulation. In Table 5, appearance reprojection alone essentially matches the full method's object-level results, while removing the geometric change score improves object/scene AP by 2.6 points. This does not undermine geometric registration, but it weakens the case for combining all three change cues. Likewise, DINOv1/v2 outperform DINOv3 on object/image AP, so the claim that the framework naturally improves with newer foundation models needs qualification.

The strongest claim concerns scene-level object consistency, but comparisons at this level are limited to the weak VLM and 3DGS-CD baselines. Applying a common association backend to competitive per-image detectors would better isolate SceneDiff's contribution. Ablations of region pooling, voxel consistency, and the association procedure are also missing; the current experiments primarily vary backbones and scoring cues.

The benchmark needs a clearer policy for observable versus physical changes. Figure 10 explicitly shows ground truth containing movements that cannot be distinguished from a simpler explanation using the available images. The manuscript does not explain whether such cases are excluded, marked ambiguous, or penalized during evaluation. Quantitative annotation-quality checks and a precise formula for aggregating scene-level IoU would further strengthen the benchmark's reliability.

The demonstrated capability remains limited: change-type-aware scene AP is 18.5 on SD-V and 7.7 on SD-K, and inference averages 159.4 seconds per sequence pair on an A40. The robot example demonstrates feasibility but provides no repeated-trial success rates. These limitations do not negate the benchmark or comparative gains, but they constrain claims of practical deployment readiness.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful computer vision problem: identifying persistent object changes across independently captured videos despite viewpoint differences and occlusions. Under Algorithms/General, the combined benchmark and method contribution supports acceptance.

The benchmark provides valuable coverage beyond existing datasets: 350 video pairs from 50 physical scenes, consistent cross-view instance annotations, and scene-level evaluation. Combining deliberately collected scenes with naturally occurring kitchen changes strengthens its relevance. Splitting by physical scene appropriately reduces leakage.

The training-free pipeline is coherent and well motivated. Joint geometric alignment, directional visibility reasoning, region-level appearance comparison, and instance association form a practical solution using clearly attributed pretrained components.

The experimental gains are substantial: object/image AP reaches 43.8 versus 24.5 on SD-V and 20.9 versus 16.8 on SD-K against finetuned CYWS-2D. RC-3D AP50 reaches 65.3 versus 50.0 for the sensor-depth baseline. Results on PASLCD and ChangeSim provide useful evidence of transfer beyond the proposed benchmark.

The supplement meaningfully strengthens the evidence through baseline implementation details, threshold sensitivity, change-type-aware evaluation, runtime measurements, and concrete failure analyses. The discussion of ambiguous identical objects and reconstruction failures is appropriately candid.
weaknesses: The ablations do not fully establish the necessity of the proposed combination. In Table 5, removing the geometry change score improves scene-level AP by 2.6 points, and the reprojected appearance score alone matches the full method's scene-level AP. Region pooling, voxel consistency, and instance association are not independently ablated. A controlled baseline sharing the same foundation models would better isolate the algorithmic contribution.

Claims that performance naturally improves as foundation models advance are too broad. Table 5 shows that DINOv1 and DINOv2 outperform DINOv3 on object/image AP, although DINOv3 improves scene-level AP. The evidence supports modularity and sensitivity to backbone quality, rather than monotonic improvement.

The central scene-level capability remains only partly validated. Its strongest comparisons are against relatively weak VLM and 3DGS baselines; attaching the same association procedure to a competitive per-view detector would make the comparison more informative. Change-type-aware AP falls to 18.5 on SD-V and 7.7 on SD-K, so reliable moved/added/removed identification remains challenging. This qualifies practical readiness without negating the benchmark's value.

Benchmark quality assurance needs more detail. Manual review of propagated masks is described, but there is no quantitative annotation audit or agreement analysis, and the rules for unverifiable changes under incomplete coverage are insufficiently explicit. With 350 pairs drawn from only 50 scenes, scene-level uncertainty estimates would also help assess generalization and smaller performance differences.

Some implementation details need clarification for reproducibility. Equation (4) pools the raw geometry score without the directional visibility mask despite the stated asymmetric rule, leaving the handling of occluded and out-of-frame pixels unclear. The SAM whole/part-mask conversion and voxel aggregation settings also need fuller specification. The supplied PDF mentions accompanying code, but that code was not available in the reviewed material.
